text: Annie Jump Cannon (December 11, 1863 – April 13, 1941) was an American astronomer whose cataloging work was essential to the development of modern stellar classification. Alongside Edward C. Pickering, she developed the Harvard Classification Scheme, the first systematic effort to classify stars based on temperature and spectral type. Cannon became nearly deaf after 1893 due to scarlet fever, which affected her social life and led her to focus intensely on her research. Born in Dover, Delaware, she was the eldest of three daughters of Wilson Cannon, a shipbuilder and state senator, and Mary Jump; her mother introduced her to astronomy and encouraged her to study mathematics, chemistry, and biology at Wellesley College. Using an old astronomy textbook, Cannon and her mother identified stars from their attic, and her mother also taught her household economics, which she applied to organize her research. At Wilmington Conference Academy and later Wellesley College, Cannon excelled in mathematics and became valedictorian, graduating with a physics degree in 1884. She developed skills in photography during a 1892 trip through Europe, and her photos and writings from Spain were published in a pamphlet titled "In the Footsteps of Columbus" for the 1893 Chicago World's Columbian Exposition. After her mother’s death in 1894, Cannon sought employment through her former instructor, Sarah Frances Whiting, who hired her as a junior physics teacher at Wellesley, allowing her to take graduate courses and learn spectroscopy. In 1894, she enrolled at Radcliffe College as a "special student" to access the Harvard College Observatory. In 1896, Pickering hired her as an assistant at the Observatory and she joined the Harvard Computers, a group of women tasked with completing the Henry Draper Catalogue, which aimed to map and classify every star to a photographic magnitude of about 9. Cannon used "Int" in her notes to denote brightness. By 1913, she could classify 200 stars per hour, classifying three stars per minute by spectral patterns and even identifying stars down to the ninth magnitude using a magnifying glass. Her work was highly accurate. Initially, disagreements arose over star classification, with Nettie Farrar leaving early, and conflicting approaches from Antonia Maury and Williamina Fleming; Cannon resolved this by applying a new system dividing stars into spectral classes O, B, A, F, G, K, M based on Balmer absorption lines, which later aligned with stellar temperature. In 1901, she published her first catalog of stellar spectra. Despite initial criticism for being outside traditional gender roles, Cannon gained respect through her "tidiness" and patience, and she helped men in the observatory gain recognition by facilitating international partnerships. In 1911, she became Curator of Astronomical Photographs at Harvard; in 1914, she was admitted as an honorary member of the Royal Astronomical Society; in 1921, she received an honorary doctorate in math and astronomy from Groningen University; in 1925, she became the first woman to receive an honorary doctorate of science from Oxford University. On May 9, 1922, the International Astronomical Union formally adopted her stellar classification system, which remains in use today with minor adjustments. In 1922, she spent six months in Arequipa, Peru, photographing southern hemisphere stars. In 1933, she represented professional women at the Chicago World's Fair (Century of Progress), and in 1935, she established the Annie J. Cannon Prize for distinguished contributions by women in astronomy. In 1938, she became the William C. Bond Astronomer at Harvard. Cecilia Payne collaborated with Cannon and used her data to demonstrate that stars are primarily composed of hydrogen and helium. Cannon’s career spanned over 40 years, ending with retirement in 1940, but she continued working actively in the observatory until shortly before her death. She classified approximately 350,000 stars in her lifetime, discovered 300 variable stars, five novas, and one spectroscopic binary, and compiled a bibliography of about 200,000 references. She died on April 13, 1941, in Cambridge, Massachusetts, at age 77, after being ill for over a month. The American Astronomical Society awards the Annie Jump Cannon Award annually to female astronomers for distinguished work in astronomy.
